mods.title: Sodium
mods.reason: Replaces Minecraft's chunk renderer with a much faster one; usually the single biggest FPS boost you can get.

mods.title: Lithium
mods.reason: Speeds up game logic such as mob AI, block ticking and collisions, so your singleplayer world spends less time on each tick.

mods.title: FerriteCore
mods.reason: Cuts the memory Minecraft uses for block and model data, which means fewer stutters while the game frees up memory.

mods.title: ModernFix-mVUS
mods.reason: Makes the game start faster and use less memory. This is the community build for current Minecraft versions, because the original ModernFix has no release for them.

mods.title: ImmediatelyFast
mods.reason: Speeds up drawing the HUD, text, items and other on-screen elements, which helps most in busy menus and around lots of signs or name tags.

mods.title: Entity Culling
mods.reason: Skips drawing mobs, chests and other entities hidden behind walls, which raises FPS in bases, villages and farms.

mods.title: More Culling
mods.reason: Skips drawing even more things you can't see, such as hidden leaf faces and item frames, on top of what Sodium and Entity Culling already skip.

mods.title: Better Block Entities
mods.reason: Draws chests, signs, beds and similar blocks much more cheaply, which helps a lot in storage rooms and large bases.

mods.title: Ixeris
mods.reason: Handles window and input events on a separate thread, which can smooth out frame times. On Windows it also reads raw mouse input in batches, which helps most with a high-polling-rate mouse; per its changelog, that part isn't ported to Minecraft 26.3's new SDL window system yet, so the gain there is smaller.

mods.title: BadOptimizations
mods.reason: A set of small client-side optimisations, such as skipping lighting and sky-colour updates when nothing has changed. It isn't part of the popular optimisation modpacks, so it starts unticked.

mods.title: ScalableLux
mods.reason: A faster lighting engine based on Starlight, so loading chunks and changing blocks costs less CPU time.

mods.title: C2ME
mods.reason: Generates and loads chunks on several CPU cores at once, so new terrain appears faster while you explore.

mods.title: Moonrise
mods.reason: Replaces the chunk system and parts of entity handling for the built-in server. It can't be used together with C2ME or ScalableLux, so RigTune doesn't suggest adding it.

mods.title: Krypton
mods.reason: Optimises Minecraft's networking code. The gain on your side is small and mostly shows on busy multiplayer servers.

mods.title: Structure Layout Optimizer
mods.reason: Speeds up how jigsaw structures like villages, bastions and ancient cities generate, which cuts stutter from worldgen on your singleplayer world's built-in server.

mods.title: Fast Noise
mods.reason: Speeds up vanilla's terrain noise generation, which cuts stutter from worldgen on your singleplayer world's built-in server. Its own issue tracker reports a rare chunk-generation crash when Lithium and C2ME are both installed, so it's off by default when C2ME is present.

mods.title: Material Rule Compiler
mods.reason: Compiles vanilla's surface-generation material rules into faster code, which cuts stutter from worldgen on your singleplayer world's built-in server. From the same project as Fast Noise, with the same rare chunk-generation crash risk when C2ME is installed.

mods.title: Async Logger
mods.reason: Moves Minecraft's log writing off the main thread and filters noisy log spam, which avoids small stutters from disk I/O.

mods.title: Dynamic FPS
mods.reason: Lowers the frame rate while Minecraft is in the background or minimised, which saves power, reduces heat and frees your PC for other apps.

mods.title: Sodium Extra
mods.reason: Adds extra video options to Sodium, such as turning off individual animations, particles or fog, so you can trade looks for FPS.

mods.title: Nvidium
mods.reason: Replaces Sodium's terrain renderer with one built on NVIDIA mesh shaders, which can greatly raise FPS at high render distances.
mods.avoidReason: Nvidium needs an NVIDIA GTX 16-series or RTX graphics card (Turing or newer, for mesh shaders) and switches itself off while a shader pack is on, so it can't help on this setup.

mods.title: RenderScale
mods.reason: Renders the game at a lower internal resolution and upscales it, which cuts GPU work on weak or integrated graphics, or on a mid-range graphics card driving a 1440p or larger screen, at the cost of some sharpness.
mods.avoidReason: Players have reported Distant Horizons terrain rendering in front of everything else when RenderScale runs together with Iris shaders.

v1.reason: Renders the game at a lower internal resolution and upscales it, which cuts GPU work on weak or integrated graphics at the cost of some sharpness.

mods.title: VulkanMod
mods.reason: Replaces Minecraft's renderer with its own Vulkan renderer. It can't run alongside Sodium or Iris and has no Minecraft 26.2 release, so RigTune doesn't suggest adding it.

mods.title: FastQuit
mods.reason: Takes you back to the title screen straight away while your world finishes saving in the background.

mods.title: Debugify
mods.reason: Fixes a long list of known vanilla bugs. Only a few affect performance, so it starts unticked.

mods.title: Particle Core
mods.reason: Skips particles you can't see and makes particle-heavy moments like explosions, fireworks and potion effects cheaper to draw.

mods.title: LambDynamicLights
mods.reason: Makes held, worn and dropped light sources such as torches and glowstone light up the area around them as they move. It's a visual feature rather than a performance one, so RigTune doesn't suggest adding it.
mods.avoidReason: LambDynamicLights keeps relighting the area around moving light sources, which costs CPU time that entry-level hardware is short of. Disabling it can win back some frame rate; if you'd rather keep the effect, pick a less smooth dynamic lighting mode in its settings instead. It starts unticked because it's a visual choice.

mods.title: Distant Horizons
mods.reason: Draws far-away terrain as simplified chunks beyond the vanilla render distance. RigTune doesn't suggest adding it; this rule tells RigTune how to treat it when it's installed.

obsolete.title: Indium
obsolete.reason: Indium's job has been built into Sodium since version 0.6, and the separate mod conflicts with current Sodium.

obsolete.title: Starlight
obsolete.reason: Minecraft's own lighting engine has included Starlight's improvements since 1.20, and Starlight has no build for this version.

obsolete.title: Phosphor
obsolete.reason: Phosphor was replaced by Starlight years ago, whose improvements are now part of Minecraft itself, and it doesn't work on current versions.

obsolete.title: OptiFabric
obsolete.reason: OptiFabric (OptiFine on Fabric) is incompatible with Sodium and hasn't been updated since Minecraft 1.20.4.

obsolete.title: LazyDFU
obsolete.reason: Minecraft now starts its data fixer efficiently by itself, so LazyDFU no longer helps, and it has no build for this version.

obsolete.title: Smooth Boot
obsolete.reason: Smooth Boot is abandoned, and changing thread priorities at start-up gives no benefit with modern Windows, macOS or Linux schedulers.

advice.title: No graphics driver in use
advice.text: Minecraft is being drawn by your CPU instead of a graphics card, which usually means the graphics driver is missing or broken, or you're in a virtual machine or remote desktop. Install the latest driver from NVIDIA, AMD or Intel and restart; no mod or setting can fix this.

advice.title: Give Minecraft more memory
advice.text: Your launcher lets Minecraft use about 2 GB of memory or less, which causes stutter as the game keeps freeing memory. Set it to at least 4 GB in your launcher's Java or memory settings.

advice.title: Low system memory
advice.text: This PC has less than 6 GB of RAM. Don't give Minecraft more than about half of it; closing your browser and other apps while playing helps more.

advice.title: Minecraft has too much of your RAM
advice.text: Minecraft is allowed to use most of this PC's memory, which leaves too little for your system and graphics driver and can cause stutter. 3 to 4 GB is enough on an 8 GB PC.

advice.title: Very large memory allocation
advice.text: Giving Minecraft 12 GB or more can make memory clean-up pauses longer on older CPUs. Unless you use a large modpack or shaders with Distant Horizons, 6 to 8 GB is plenty.

advice.title: Distant Horizons needs more memory
advice.text: Distant Horizons keeps far-away terrain in memory and, per its FAQ, needs roughly 2 to 4 GB more than vanilla. Allocate at least 6 GB in your launcher.

advice.title: Shaders need more memory
advice.text: Shader packs use extra memory, and with less than 6 GB for Minecraft you may get stutter. Allocate 6 GB in your launcher.

advice.title: Distant Horizons with shaders needs more memory
advice.text: Distant Horizons with a shader pack is one of the heaviest setups. You have plenty of RAM, so allocate about 8 GB to Minecraft in your launcher.

advice.title: Distant Horizons with shaders needs more memory
advice.text: Distant Horizons with a shader pack is one of the heaviest setups: per its FAQ, Distant Horizons alone needs roughly 2 to 4 GB more memory than vanilla, and the shader pack adds more. Allocate 6 GB in your launcher. This PC has less than 16 GB of RAM, so don't go much higher; keep Distant Horizons' render distance moderate instead.

advice.title: Distant Horizons on a PC with little RAM
advice.text: Per its FAQ, Distant Horizons needs roughly 2 to 4 GB more memory than vanilla, but this PC has less than 12 GB of RAM, so give Minecraft about 4 GB at most. Keep Distant Horizons' render distance short instead, and close other apps while you play.

advice.title: Running on battery
advice.text: Laptops slow down the CPU and GPU on battery to save power, so expect lower FPS. Plug in for full performance, or keep RigTune's battery-saving settings.

advice.title: Check which graphics chip Minecraft uses
advice.text: Minecraft is running on integrated graphics. If this laptop also has a dedicated graphics card, set Java (javaw.exe) to High performance in Windows Settings > System > Display > Graphics, then restart the game.

advice.title: Experimental Vulkan renderer
advice.text: Minecraft is using its experimental Vulkan renderer, which can be slower or less stable on some PCs, and some mods may not support it yet. If you have problems, set Video Settings > Graphics API back to Default and restart.

advice.title: Update your Intel graphics driver
advice.text: Older Intel integrated graphics have crash and flicker bugs that are only fixed in Intel's own drivers. Install the newest driver from Intel's website instead of relying on Windows Update.

advice.title: Shaders are heavy for this GPU
advice.text: A shader pack is on, and on this graphics card shaders usually cost more FPS than every other setting combined. Try a lighter pack or a lower shader quality preset, or turn shaders off in Video Settings > Shader Packs.

advice.title: Shaders are heavy for this PC
advice.text: A shader pack is on, and at this hardware level shaders usually cost more FPS than every other setting combined. Turn shaders off in Video Settings > Shader Packs, or switch to a pack made for low-end PCs, such as MakeUp - Ultra Fast.

advice.title: Shader packs that support Distant Horizons
advice.text: A shader pack needs built-in Distant Horizons support to draw Distant Horizons' far terrain properly. Two community compatibility lists agree that Complementary Reimagined, Complementary Unbound, BSL (8.2.0 or newer), Bliss and Photon support it; community guides rate Complementary Unbound and Photon as the heaviest of these.

advice.title: NVIDIA Threaded Optimization detected
advice.text: Your NVIDIA driver applies a Threaded Optimization feature that Sodium reports causes stutter and crashes with Minecraft, and Sodium is working around it. If you still get stutter or crashes, try a launcher the driver doesn't recognise, such as Prism Launcher.

advice.title: AMD driver issue handled by Sodium
advice.text: Your AMD driver applies a Minecraft-specific tweak that can make terrain invisible. Sodium hides the game from that driver check automatically, so you don't need to do anything.

advice.title: Intel driver issue handled by Sodium
advice.text: Your Intel graphics driver can crash when the game window loses focus. Sodium works around this, and installing the newest driver from Intel's website can help too.

advice.title: Intel depth-buffer issue handled by Sodium
advice.text: Your Intel graphics has a depth-buffer bug that can make surfaces flicker. Sodium works around it automatically.

advice.title: OpenGL setting adjusted by Sodium
advice.text: Your system doesn't support one of OpenGL's faster error-checking modes (common on Linux with Wayland), so Sodium turned it off to avoid a crash at start-up. You don't need to do anything.

advice.title: Find what causes lag with spark
advice.text: Run /sparkc profiler start, play through the lag, then /sparkc profiler stop and open the link it prints: under Render thread, the highest percentages cost the most time. Stopping uploads the profile to spark.lucko.me with your player name and UUID, mod list, system details and Java launch arguments; anyone with the link can see it.

advice.title: Java ignores some of your Java arguments
advice.text: Java doesn't use some of the flags in your Java arguments: they were removed from Java, or they don't work on this PC. They do nothing now, and a removed flag can stop a later Java from starting (OpenJDK says so for -XX:+ZGenerational). Remove them from your Java arguments.

advice.title: Fixed young-generation size in your Java arguments
advice.text: Your Java arguments fix the size of Java's young generation (-Xmn, NewSize or MaxNewSize). Java's own G1 tuning guide says that "overrides and practically disables pause-time control", the part of the garbage collector that keeps its pauses short. Remove it from your Java arguments.

advice.title: Your Java arguments pick a collector that pauses the game
advice.text: Your Java arguments switch Java to its Serial or Parallel garbage collector, which stop the game for every collection. Java's own documentation suggests Parallel only when "pauses of one second or longer are acceptable". Remove -XX:+UseSerialGC or -XX:+UseParallelGC so Java uses its default collector, G1.

advice.title: Java is set to never free memory
advice.text: Your Java arguments turn on Epsilon (-XX:+UseEpsilonGC), a garbage collector that never frees memory: Minecraft will run out of memory and crash. Remove it from your Java arguments.

advice.title: Server flags in your Java arguments
advice.text: These are Paper's server flags ("Aikar's flags") or a set based on them. In RigTune's tests they gave the same frame rates and 1% lows as Java's defaults, but with the -Xms usually pasted with them Minecraft kept its whole memory allocation reserved even when it didn't need it (all 4096 MB of a 4 GB allocation, against about 1.3 GB with Java's defaults). On a PC with 16 GB of RAM or less, remove these flags and keep only your launcher's memory setting.

advice.title: Explicit garbage collection is turned off
advice.text: -XX:+DisableExplicitGC stops Minecraft's out-of-memory recovery and Java's direct-memory cleanup from asking for a garbage collection, and it brings no benefit in play. Remove it from your Java arguments.

advice.title: ZGC with little memory
advice.text: Java's ZGC guide says ZGC works better the more memory it gets, and it keeps almost all of that memory in use. On RigTune's test PC, ZGC with 2 GB gave slightly lower 1% lows than with 4 GB. This PC has room for 4 GB. The options: 4 GB in your launcher's memory setting, or removing -XX:+UseZGC, which returns to Java's default collector (G1).

advice.title: ZGC on a PC with 8 GB of RAM or less
advice.text: ZGC keeps almost its whole heap committed: on RigTune's test PC it kept 3.9 of 4 GB, against about 1.3 GB for Java's default collector (G1). On a PC with 8 GB of RAM or less, that leaves less memory for everything else. ZGC is the official Minecraft Launcher's default since 26.1, so this may not be something you changed. If the game or the PC feels slow, removing -XX:+UseZGC returns to G1.

advice.title: Memory is set more than once
advice.text: Your Java arguments set the maximum memory (-Xmx) more than once, and Java uses only the last one, so the memory your launcher shows may not be what Minecraft gets. Keep only one: remove the extra -Xmx from your Java arguments.

advice.title: Update your NVIDIA graphics driver
advice.text: NVIDIA drivers 526.47 to 536.22 force Threaded Optimization for Minecraft, which Sodium reports causes crashes and stutter (Sodium issue #1486). Update your graphics driver.

advice.title: Intel HD Graphics driver too old for Sodium
advice.text: Intel HD Graphics drivers older than 10.18.10.5161 can freeze Minecraft at startup with Sodium (Sodium issue #899); update the driver.

settings.reason: Max FPS takes the frame-rate cap off.
VSync would hold the frame rate at your monitor's refresh rate.
Shader packs multiply the GPU's work, which drains the battery fastest.
Turning Distant Horizons' rendering off saves the GPU work of drawing its far terrain.
Clouds off saves GPU work on battery.
Fewer chunks mean less CPU and GPU work on battery.
A shorter simulation distance means less CPU work on battery.
Fewer particles save GPU work on battery.
A steady frame rate at a usual recording rate (60 FPS, or your display's rate below that) leaves headroom for the recording software.
On a display of 60 Hz or less the cap is at or below the refresh rate, so VSync stops tearing at little cost.
Above 60 Hz, VSync would add input lag on top of the 60 FPS cap.
Keeps the full frame rate during idle or cinematic shots instead of lowering it after a minute without input.
Deferred chunk updates never make a frame wait for chunk building, for even frame times; blocks may take a moment to appear.
The Threaded chunk builder doesn't make frames wait for chunk building, for even frame times.

stutterAdvice.title: Stutter likely linked to low memory
stutterAdvice.text: Garbage-collection pauses took a large share of the time lost to stutter, and Minecraft's memory was nearly full, so it likely needs more. Give Minecraft about 2 GB more in your launcher's memory setting; this PC has room for it. Switching the garbage collector or adding GC flags likely isn't the fix: in RigTune's tests they gave no frame-rate gain over Java's defaults, so more memory is the change to try first.

stutterAdvice.title: Something asks Java for full garbage collections
stutterAdvice.text: Some of the stutter overlapped full garbage collections that were requested on purpose (System.gc()). Minecraft itself doesn't do that in normal play, so a mod, or Java freeing direct memory, likely asked for them. If the stutter started after you added or updated a mod, try the game without it.

stutterAdvice.title: Frames wait for chunk updates
stutterAdvice.text: Chunk building likely took part in a good share of the stutter, and Sodium's Chunk Updates setting makes frames wait for it. Set Chunk Updates to Deferred in Sodium's video settings (Performance page): frames stop waiting, though changed blocks may take a moment to appear.

stutterAdvice.title: Distant Horizons may compete for the CPU
stutterAdvice.text: Distant Horizons was busy during many of the spikes while the CPU was heavily loaded, so they may be related. While you explore new terrain, try a lower "NO. of threads" in Distant Horizons' settings: it builds far terrain more slowly but leaves more CPU for the game.

stutterAdvice.title: Stutter while loading chunks
stutterAdvice.text: Loading new chunks likely took part in a large share of the stutter. A render distance 2 to 4 chunks shorter loads fewer chunks at a time. If you fly or teleport a lot in singleplayer, pre-generating the world (for example with the Chunky mod) means the game no longer has to generate new terrain while you play.
